questions.question: What is CRUD and how does ActiveRecord do it?
questions.title: ActiveRecord CRUD Basics
questions.direct_answer: CRUD means Create, Read, Update, and Delete. Active Record maps those database operations to model objects and methods: `new` builds without saving, `create` builds and attempts an INSERT, finders read rows, `update` changes attributes and attempts an UPDATE, and `destroy` removes a record while running destroy callbacks. Normal persistence methods run validations and return a result that must be checked; bang methods such as `save!` raise when persistence fails.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the four CRUD operations and the ActiveRecord methods for each (create/save/find/where/update/destroy).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using delete instead of destroy (delete skips callbacks), or not saving after new.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: CRUD = Create/Read/Update/Delete; ActiveRecord maps them to create+save, find/where, update, destroy. destroy (not delete) runs callbacks.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `new` builds an unsaved object; `create` builds and tries to persist it.
- `find(id)` raises when absent; `find_by(...)` returns one record or `nil`.
- `save` and `update` return success status after validations and callbacks.
- Bang forms such as `save!` and `update!` raise on validation failure.
- `destroy` runs callbacks; `delete` removes directly and skips them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
CRUD means Create, Read, Update, and Delete. Active Record maps those database operations to Ruby model objects and methods. The API is convenient, but each method still has a clear persistence, validation, callback, and failure contract that the caller must understand.

`Article.new(...)` builds an in-memory object and does not insert a row. `save` validates it and returns `true` or `false`; `save!` raises on validation failure. `Article.create(...)` combines building and saving but can still return an invalid, unpersisted object, so check the result rather than assuming success.

For reading, `Article.find(id)` returns the required primary-key record or raises `RecordNotFound`; `find_by(...)` returns one match or `nil`. `update(...)` validates and returns a Boolean, while `update!(...)` raises when the write is invalid. Pick the form that matches normal versus exceptional control flow.

A loaded record can call `update(title: "Revised")`, which assigns values, validates, runs callbacks, and attempts an UPDATE. `destroy` runs the destroy lifecycle and configured association behavior. `delete` removes directly and skips that lifecycle, so it belongs only in code that intentionally accepts those missing callbacks.

CRUD methods make one-record work readable; they do not make a multi-record business operation atomic by themselves. If an article and its audit row must both change or neither may change, wrap them in one database transaction and use a failure form that causes the transaction to roll back.

article = Article.new(title: "Active Record basics")

if article.save
  puts "created #{article.id}"
else
  puts article.errors.full_messages
end
support.caption: The non-bang save path keeps validation errors on the object and reports failure without raising.

Pick the form that matches normal versus exceptional control flow.

items.detail: create still returns the object when validation blocks persistence.

items.label: find / find_by

items.label: save / save!

sections.title: An object moves between new, persisted, changed, and destroyed states
sections.content:
An Active Record instance represents one row plus in-memory state. Before the first successful save it has no database identity. A successful INSERT assigns its primary key and clears tracked changes; later assignments remain in memory until another persistence method writes an UPDATE.

Validation and callback chains surround normal writes. A failed validation stops the SQL write but leaves the attempted values and error messages on the object. Bang and non-bang methods run the same model rules; they differ mainly in whether failure becomes an exception or a false return value.

Finder contracts matter at control-flow boundaries. `find` is appropriate when the record must exist and absence should take an exception path. `find_by` is appropriate when absence is a normal alternative the caller will branch on. Both still issue a query when evaluated.

Deletion has two meanings. Destroying asks the model to perform its lifecycle, including callbacks and configured dependent associations. Deleting issues a direct removal that bypasses that model lifecycle. The faster-looking method can leave related data or side effects inconsistent if the lifecycle was part of the contract.

sections.title: Complete Rails example: create, find, update, and destroy one article
sections.content:
```ruby
class Article < ApplicationRecord
  validates :title, presence: true
end

article = Article.new(title: "Active Record basics")
if article.save
  puts "created #{article.id}"
else
  abort article.errors.full_messages.join(", ")
end

found = Article.find(article.id)
found.update!(published: true)
puts found.published?

found.destroy
puts found.destroyed?
```

When should a finder return `nil`, and when should it raise?
Why can replacing `destroy` with `delete` change application behaviour?

questions.question: How do you query records with ActiveRecord?
questions.title: ActiveRecord Basic Querying
questions.direct_answer: Active Record queries are built by chaining relation methods such as `where`, `order`, `select`, `limit`, and `joins`. Most of these return an `ActiveRecord::Relation`, which stores a query plan and can be refined before SQL is executed when records are actually needed. `find` and `find_by` return individual model objects with different missing-record behaviour. Hash conditions and placeholder parameters keep values bound safely; interpolating untrusted input into SQL can create SQL injection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the chainable query methods (where/order/limit/first/find) and that they return a relation you can chain until a terminal call.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling .all and loading everything, or using raw SQL with interpolation where a query method is safer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: where/order/limit/first/find are chainable and return a Relation; chain until a terminal method (first, to_a, each) runs the SQL.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `where` returns a chainable relation, not one model object.
- Relations are normally lazy until records or aggregate results are needed.
- `find(id)` raises when absent; `find_by(...)` returns a record or `nil`.
- Chain `where`, `order`, `limit`, and `select` to express one query.
- Bind untrusted values with hashes or placeholders instead of SQL interpolation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Active Record builds database queries with chainable methods such as `where`, `order`, `limit`, `select`, and `joins`. Most collection methods return an `ActiveRecord::Relation`: a description that can be refined and passed to another method before matching rows are loaded.

`Article.where(published: true).order(created_at: :desc).limit(5)` expresses filtering, ordering, and limiting in one relation. Use hash conditions or placeholders such as `where("price >= ?", minimum)` for input values. String interpolation lets untrusted text change SQL and can create injection vulnerabilities.

A relation is usually lazy until code needs a result. Calling `each`, `to_a`, or `first` loads records; operations such as `count`, `exists?`, and `pluck(:id)` run smaller specialised queries. Calling `to_a` too early moves later filtering into Ruby and may load far more data than necessary.

`find(id)` returns a required primary-key record and raises when it is absent. `find_by(slug: value)` returns the first match or `nil`; add an order when several rows could match and the chosen row matters. Inspect `to_sql` and query logs when generated SQL or performance is unclear.

A good parent relation can still create N+1 queries if a view later reads unloaded associations. Load only the relationships the response uses and give pagination a stable order. Query construction should reduce database work while still returning the exact model objects or scalar values the caller needs.

beats.cue: Define a Relation as a query description that remains composable
beats.spokenText: Active Record builds database queries with chainable methods such as `where`, `order`, `limit`, `select`, and `joins`. Most collection methods return an `ActiveRecord::Relation`: a description that can be refined and passed to another method before matching rows are loaded.

beats.cue: Build one bounded query while keeping values separate from SQL
beats.spokenText: `Article.where(published: true).order(created_at: :desc).limit(5)` expresses filtering, ordering, and limiting in one relation. Use hash conditions or placeholders such as `where("price >= ?", minimum)` for input values. String interpolation lets untrusted text change SQL and can create injection vulnerabilities.

support.title: Compose one safe and bounded article query
support.code:
recent = Article
  .where(published: true, author_id: author_id)
  .where("created_at >= ?", since)
  .order(created_at: :desc)
  .limit(5)
support.caption: Each chain adds one database clause; values stay bound separately from SQL structure.

Calling `each`, `to_a`, or `first` loads records; operations such as `count`, `exists?`, and `pluck(:id)` run smaller specialised queries. Calling `to_a` too early moves later filtering into Ruby and may load far more data than necessary.

items.label: where
items.detail: The relation is still open to more database clauses.

items.label: order and limit

items.label: each or to_a

items.label: pluck or exists?

beats.spokenText: `find(id)` returns a required primary-key record and raises when it is absent. `find_by(slug: value)` returns the first match or `nil`; add an order when several rows could match and the chosen row matters. sections.title: A relation is a composable query description
sections.content:
An `ActiveRecord::Relation` holds clauses and model metadata rather than immediately loading every matching row. Each chain call produces a relation with another part of the intended SQL. This lets a reusable scope contribute one condition while its caller adds pagination or ordering.

Execution boundaries differ. Iteration loads records; `count`, `exists?`, and `pluck` can ask the database for a smaller result; `first` adds a limit. Calling `to_a` early replaces the database's filtering options with in-memory Ruby work and can load far more rows than necessary.

Selecting columns affects the model objects returned. `pluck(:id)` returns plain values, which is efficient when no model behaviour is required. `select(:id, :title)` returns partial model instances, and reading an omitted attribute may fail, so that optimisation must stay within a narrow boundary.

Query values and SQL structure are separate concerns. Bound parameters let the database adapter quote values correctly and prevent an input string from becoming executable SQL. Dynamic column names or sort directions require allowlists because placeholders bind values, not arbitrary SQL identifiers.

sections.title: Complete Rails example: return recent articles for one author
sections.content:
```ruby
class RecentArticles
  def self.for_author(author_id:, since:, limit: 5)
    Article
      .where(published: true, author_id: author_id)
      .where("created_at >= ?", since)
      .order(created_at: :desc)
      .limit(limit)
  end
end

recent = RecentArticles.for_author(
  author_id: 4,
  since: 30.days.ago,
  limit: 5
)

puts recent.to_sql
recent.each { |article| puts article.title }
```
